title: Script traps: what does it really do?
about: Single-choice questions on the traps that cost points in a script and in the test: word splitting, quoting, empty variables, subshells, redirection order, exit statuses, find and tests. Every output was run in the lab.

questions.title: Looping over ls
questions.text:
A directory holds three files: `a.txt`, `b.txt` and `my notes.txt`. How many times does this loop run?

```bash
for f in $(ls); do echo "got: $f"; done
```

options.t: 4 times, because `my notes.txt` is split into the two words `my` and `notes.txt`.
options.why: The unquoted `$(ls)` is split on spaces; use `for f in ./*` (or `find`) to keep names whole.

options.t: 3 times, once per file, because `ls` prints one name per line and the loop reads lines.
options.why: A `for` loop iterates over words, not lines.

options.t: 2 times, because the shell groups the two names that contain a dot into one word.
options.why: The shell never groups words by their characters.

options.t: 0 times, because `$(ls)` is only expanded inside double quotes.
options.why: Command substitution works unquoted too; it is then split into words.

questions.title: An empty variable inside [ ]
questions.text:
In a script `x` is empty (`x=`). What happens with this line?

```bash
[ $x = yes ]
```

options.t: The test fails with an error (`unary operator expected`) and a status of 2.
options.why: Unquoted, the empty `$x` disappears and `[` sees only `= yes`.

options.t: It is simply false, with status 1, because an empty string is different from `yes`.
options.why: That would be the result with `[ "$x" = yes ]`; unquoted there is a syntax error instead.

options.t: It is true, because an empty variable compares equal to anything.
options.why: Nothing compares equal to everything in the shell.

options.t: The shell stops with `x: unbound variable`, as the variable was never given a value.
options.why: Unset or empty variables only raise that error under `set -u`.

questions.title: -n with an unquoted empty variable
questions.text:
What does this print?

```bash
y=
[ -n $y ]
echo $?
```

options.t: `0`: with `$y` unquoted the test becomes `[ -n ]`, which only checks that the string `-n` is not empty.
options.why: Quote it, `[ -n "$y" ]`, and the answer is `1`.

options.t: `1`, because `-n` is true only when the string after it is not empty, and `y` is empty here.
options.why: That is the result of `[ -n "$y" ]`, with the quotes.

options.t: `2`, because after the expansion `[ -n ]` is an incomplete test and a syntax error.
options.why: `[ -n ]` has one argument, and a single non-empty argument is true.

options.t: Nothing is printed, because `[` stops the whole script when its test is badly written.
options.why: `echo $?` always prints the status of the last command.

questions.title: Spaces in an assignment
questions.text:
What happens with this line in a script?

```bash
file=my file.txt
```

options.t: The shell runs the command `file.txt` with `file=my` in its environment, so it prints `file.txt: command not found`.
options.why: A space ends the assignment; quote the value: `file="my file.txt"`.

options.t: The variable `file` is assigned the two words `my file.txt`, spaces included, as in any language.
options.why: Only quotes (or a backslash) keep the space inside the value.

options.t: The shell reports a syntax error on that line and runs nothing at all from the script.
options.why: It is valid syntax: a temporary assignment followed by a command.

options.t: The variable is assigned `my` and the rest of the line, from the space on, is ignored as a comment.
options.why: A comment needs `#`.

questions.title: "$@", $* and "$*"
questions.text: A script is called as `./s.sh "a b" c`. Which loop runs exactly twice, first with `a b` and then with `c`?

options.why: `"$@"` expands to one word per argument, keeping each one whole.
Unquoted, `$@` is split again: three words `a`, `b` and `c`.
`"$*"` is one single word, `a b c`, so it runs once.
Unquoted `$*` is split too: three iterations.

questions.title: Single and double quotes together
questions.text:
With `v=3`, what does this line print?

```bash
echo '$v' "$v" "\$v"
```

options.why: Single quotes and an escaped dollar print the text; only the middle word is expanded.
Single quotes stop the expansion, and so does the backslash.
Double quotes do expand `$v`.
The expansion happens in the middle word, the one in double quotes without a backslash.

questions.title: Quoting a command substitution
questions.text:
What do these two lines print?

```bash
echo "$(echo a; echo b)"
echo $(echo a; echo b)
```

options.t: First `a` and `b` on two lines, then `a b` on one line.
options.why: The quotes keep the newline; unquoted, the result is split into words that `echo` joins with a space.

options.t: `a b` both times, since `echo` always puts its arguments on one line.
options.why: Inside quotes the substitution is one single argument with a newline in it.

options.t: `a` and `b` on two lines both times, because the substitution keeps its newline.
options.why: Without quotes the newline is just a word separator.

options.t: An error, because a command substitution cannot contain a semicolon.
options.why: Any command list can go inside `$( )`.

questions.title: Plus in an assignment
questions.text:
What does this print?

```bash
x=5
y=$x+1
echo $y
```

options.why: Without `$(( ))` the value is just text.
Arithmetic needs `$(( ))` or `let`.
`$x` is expanded to its value.

options.t: Nothing: the second line is a syntax error.
options.why: It is a valid assignment of the text `5+1`.

questions.title: $1 inside a function
questions.text:
This is `s.sh`, run as `bash s.sh a`. What does it print?

```bash
f() { echo "inside: $1"; }
f b
echo "outside: $1"
```

options.why: Inside a function `$1` is the first argument of the function call; outside it is the script's.
The positional parameters are replaced inside a function.
When the function ends the script's own arguments are back.
The function receives `b`, so `$1` is not empty.

questions.title: A counter in a pipeline
questions.text:
What does this print?

```bash
n=0
printf 'a\nb\nc\n' | while read l; do n=$((n + 1)); done
echo "n=$n"
```

options.why: Each side of a pipe runs in a subshell, so the loop increments a copy of `n`.
The loop does run three times, but its variables disappear with its subshell.
The variable is not reset in each iteration; the changes are lost at the end.

options.t: An error because `read` cannot be used inside a loop.
options.why: `while read` is the usual idiom to read lines.

questions.title: read at the end of a pipe
questions.text:
What does this print?

```bash
unset x
echo hello | read x
echo "[$x]"
```

options.why: `read` runs in a subshell of the pipe, so `x` is still unset in the shell.
The assignment is made in the subshell and lost with it.
`read x` stores the text in a variable, it does not print its name.

options.t: An error: `read` cannot take its input from a pipe.
options.why: It can; the problem is where the variable lives.

questions.title: cd in a subshell
questions.text:
What do these lines print, if the script starts in `/home/alumno`?

```bash
(cd /tmp; pwd)
pwd
```

options.why: The parentheses run in a subshell, so the `cd` does not affect the script.
That would happen with braces `{ cd /tmp; pwd; }`, which run in the same shell.
Inside the subshell the `cd` does work.

options.t: An error, because `cd` is not allowed between parentheses.
options.why: Any command can run in a subshell.

questions.title: return and exit in a function
questions.text:
What does the script print, and with which exit status does it finish?

```bash
f() { return 3; echo no; }
g() { exit 4; }
f; echo "after f: $?"
g; echo "never"
```

options.t: `after f: 3`, and the script ends with status 4 without printing `never`.
options.why: `return` leaves the function; `exit` ends the whole script.

options.t: `after f: 3` and `never`, and the script ends with status 0.
options.why: `exit` inside a function terminates the script, not only the function.
Nothing after `return` in the function runs.

options.t: `after f: 0` and status 4, as `return` does not change `$?`.
options.why: `return 3` sets the status to 3.

questions.title: The status of ((n++))
questions.text:
What does this print?

```bash
n=0
((n++))
echo "$? $n"
```

options.why: The value of the expression is the old `0`, and an arithmetic command with value 0 has status 1.
The status of `(( ))` depends on the value of the expression, not on whether it worked.
The variable is incremented, so `n` is 1.
The increment is done after the value is taken, but it is done.

questions.title: Counting the arguments
questions.text:
How many arguments does the script see in the first call?

```bash
bash cnt.sh "a b" c ""     # cnt.sh: echo "args: $#"
```

options.why: Quotes group words, and an empty quoted string is still an argument.

options.t: 2, because the empty string is not an argument.
options.why: `""` is an argument with an empty value.
The quotes keep `a b` together.

options.t: 1, because `$#` counts only the first word.
options.why: `$#` is the total number of arguments.

questions.title: Sending the error into the file
questions.text: Which command stores the error message of `ls` in the file `o`, and prints nothing on the screen?

options.why: First stdout goes to `o`, then stderr is sent to wherever stdout points now.
Stderr is duplicated to the screen first; only stdout then goes to `o`, which stays empty.
Only stdout goes to `o`; the error still appears on the screen.
The later `> o` wins for stdout, and the error travels on stderr, which is never redirected: it stays on the screen and `o` is empty.

questions.title: What stays on the screen
questions.text: `s.sh` contains `echo ok` and `echo bad >&2`. What does `bash s.sh > out` do?

options.t: `out` contains `ok`, and `bad` appears on the screen.
options.why: `>&2` sends the message to stderr, which `> out` does not redirect.

options.t: `out` contains `ok` and `bad`, because both are written by `echo`.
options.why: The second `echo` writes to file descriptor 2.

options.t: `out` is empty and both words appear on the screen.
options.why: The redirection takes stdout, so `ok` goes to the file.

options.t: `out` contains `bad` and `ok` appears on the screen.
options.why: Stdout is the one that is redirected.

questions.title: && and || together
questions.text:
What does this line print?

```bash
true || echo A && echo B
```

options.why: The operators have the same precedence and group from the left: `(true || echo A) && echo B`.
`true` makes the `||` branch skip `echo A`.
`echo A` is not run because the left side succeeded.

options.t: Nothing, because the first command already succeeded.
options.why: The `&&` part still runs after a successful `true || ...`.

questions.title: Silenced does not mean succeeded
questions.text:
What does this print?

```bash
ls /nonexistent 2>/dev/null
echo $?
```

options.why: The redirection only hides the message; the status is the one of `ls`, which failed.
The status does not depend on the output.
The status is chosen by each program; `ls` uses 2 for a missing file.

options.t: Nothing, because `/dev/null` also swallows the status.
options.why: `$?` is a variable of the shell, not output.

questions.title: An unquoted pattern in find
questions.text:
The current directory has `a.txt`, `b.txt` and `c.txt`. What does this do?

```bash
find . -name *.txt
```

options.t: It fails with `paths must precede expression`, because the shell expanded `*.txt` before `find` ran.
options.why: `find` receives `-name a.txt b.txt c.txt`; quote the pattern.

options.t: It lists every `.txt` file of the whole tree, since `find` understands patterns by itself.
options.why: Only when it receives the pattern; here the shell expands it first.

options.t: It lists only `a.txt`, `b.txt` and `c.txt` of the current directory, and nothing from below.
options.why: It does not run as a search at all: it is an error.

options.t: It finds nothing and ends quietly, because the pattern was written without any quotes.
options.why: Without matching files the pattern would be passed unchanged; here there are matches.

questions.title: -o and the implicit print
questions.text:
The directory holds `p.sh` and `q.bin`. What does this print?

```bash
find . -name '*.sh' -o -name '*.bin' -print
```

options.why: The explicit `-print` applies only to the second alternative; the first one has no action.
That needs parentheses: `\( -name '*.sh' -o -name '*.bin' \) -print`.
The `-print` is attached to the `.bin` test.

options.t: An error, because `-o` cannot be mixed with `-print`.
options.why: It is valid; it just does not mean what you may expect.

questions.title: The semicolon of -exec
questions.text:
What happens with this command?

```bash
find . -name p.sh -exec echo {} ;
```

options.t: `find` stops with `missing argument to -exec`, because the shell consumed the bare `;`.
options.why: Write `\;` or `';'` so that `find` receives it.
The shell strips the semicolon before `find` sees it.
The semicolon never reaches `echo`.

options.t: It runs `find` without any action and then runs `echo` as a separate command.
options.why: The shell only splits the line at the semicolon; `find` still gets `-exec echo {}` and complains.

questions.title: Files with any execute bit
questions.text: In a directory, `q.bin` has mode 700, `r.x` has mode 010 and `p.sh` has 644. Which command lists exactly `q.bin` and `r.x`?

options.why: `/111` means "any of these bits is set".
`-111` needs all three execute bits, which neither file has.
Without a prefix the mode must be exactly 111.
It requires the owner's execute bit, so `r.x` is missed.

questions.title: Only the files directly inside
questions.text: Which line lists only the regular files directly inside `$dir`, correctly even if the names have spaces?

options.why: Limits the depth, selects regular files and does not split names.
It selects regular files, but it also goes into every subdirectory.
Unquoted it splits names at spaces, and it also keeps symbolic links and the `total` line.
The depth is right, but it also keeps symbolic links, sockets and any other non-directory.

questions.title: The size of -size +1k
questions.text: A directory holds files of 1 byte, 1024 bytes, 1025 bytes and 2049 bytes. Which ones does `find . -type f -size +1k` list?

options.why: Sizes are rounded up to whole kilobytes and `+1k` means more than one: more than 1024 bytes.

options.t: All the files, because every file is at least a kilobyte on disk.
options.why: `-size` compares the length in bytes, rounded up to the unit.
1025 bytes rounds up to 2 kilobytes, which is more than 1.
1024 bytes is exactly 1 kilobyte, which is not more than 1.

questions.title: Comparing numbers
questions.text: What does `[ 10 \< 9 ]` return?

options.t: True (status 0), because `\<` compares the two texts alphabetically and `1` comes before `9`.
options.why: For numbers use `-lt`: `[ 10 -lt 9 ]` is false.

options.t: False (status 1), because the number 10 is not smaller than the number 9.
options.why: That is what `-lt` answers; `\<` compares strings.

options.t: An error, because the `<` sign cannot be used as an operator inside `[ ]`.
options.why: Escaped, it is the string comparison operator.

options.t: True only if both operands are written between quotes, which turns them into text.
options.why: Quotes do not change which operator is used.

questions.title: = and -eq
questions.text:
What do these two tests return?

```bash
[ 01 = 1 ]; echo $?
[ 01 -eq 1 ]; echo $?
```

options.why: `=` compares texts (`01` is not `1`); `-eq` compares numbers.
Both look equal, but the first compares characters.
As numbers, 01 and 1 are the same.
The operators are swapped in this answer.

questions.title: Patterns in [[ ]]
questions.text:
With `f=a.sh`, what do these two tests return?

```bash
[[ $f == *.sh ]];   echo $?
[[ $f == "*.sh" ]]; echo $?
```

options.why: Unquoted, the right side is a pattern; quoted, it is the literal text `*.sh`.
With quotes there is no pattern, only the text `*.sh`.
It is the other way round.
The first one is a pattern and `a.sh` matches it.

questions.title: Integer arithmetic
questions.text:
What does this line print?

```bash
echo $((7 / 2)) $((7 % 2)) $((2 ** 3)) $((-7 / 2))
```

options.why: The division is whole and truncates toward zero.
The shell does integer arithmetic only.
`**` is a power, and the division truncates toward zero, not down.
The division does not round.

groups.title: Finding out what a command is

questions.title: Builtin or file
questions.text: What does `type cd` print in bash?

options.why: `cd` must change the directory of the shell itself, so it cannot be a separate program.
There is no program that could change the directory of the shell.
Keywords are words like `if` and `while`; `cd` is a normal command.
`type` knows builtins.

questions.title: The manual of a file format
questions.text: Which command shows the manual page that describes the format of the file `/etc/passwd`?

options.why: Section 5 of the manual holds the file formats.
It shows the command that changes passwords (section 1).
Section 8 is for administration commands.
It lists matching page names; it does not open the page.
